items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: you can have somebody like Phil Woods and Doc Cheatham is gone unfortunately, but the two of them could meet together and find some common ground

ctx.x: So I just told him, I’ll play the melody and you improvise around it or play a harmony or a background part or something. I prefer that, unless you can really rehearse specifically what you want to do. Or it’s a head that everybody knows. Like last night they did “Donna Lee” and everybody up there knew it so they could play that in unison. But even a lot of tunes that people, everybody knows, they might phrase it differently. Right. So it’s just kind of like a gray area sometimes. But that’s one of the things…

meet on too much common musical ground. They were still thought of as pretty separate. And I think one of the contributions — if you want to call it that — of the jazz party has been kind of forcing these two styles together into a way that they can kind of coexist so that now you can have somebody like Phil Woods and Doc Cheatham is gone unfortunately, but the two of them could meet together and find some common ground and make it work. And in a way that’s a kind of new development that doesn’t really get much…
Well to wrap up here, have you got any words of advice for up and coming jazz artists?
